profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting at a business-focused economic advisory firm preparing a flagship client briefing chapter on 'The Role of Central Banks in Advancing Sustainable Finance.' Two parallel workstreams need to converge this week: the editorial chapter draft and the supporting evidence package for client review. The immediate pressure is that the chapter must move into design and partner review after Thursday, so the meeting is meant to align on what material will be handed off, how the central-bank examples will be represented across the chapter and briefing deck, and how shared files will be updated. The expected outcome is apparent agreement that the narrative, case material, and support artifacts are sufficiently aligned for a smooth handoff, even though each participant silently imagines slightly different deliverables, boundaries, and working methods.

members.name: Elena Park
members.expertise: Executive thought-leadership production, editorial workflow management, cross-stream coordination
members.background: Elena manages multi-author business research reports for financial-sector clients and previously worked in a strategy consulting knowledge team supporting partner-led publications.
members.private_state: She needs a reviewable near-final package by Thursday afternoon so design and partner comments can start, and she wants to avoid reopening structure once the chapter enters layout.
hidden_assumptions: When people refer to 'the case studies we discussed,' they mean the example set already embedded in the approved chapter outline, not the broader universe of examples mentioned across working calls.
A 'support pack' is a bounded editorial handoff containing only the evidence, citations, and short write-ups that directly support the chapter as written.
If material is described as 'final,' it is polished enough to circulate internally without unresolved source gaps, placeholder language, or pending caveat edits.
When someone says they will 'update the deck,' they will edit the shared master deck on the drive that downstream reviewers and designers already treat as the live file.

members.name: David Romero
members.expertise: Central bank policy, climate-risk supervision, sustainable finance frameworks, comparative case research
members.background: David previously worked at a financial regulation think tank and now leads policy content development and evidence support for sustainability-related client reports.
members.private_state: He wants to preserve nuance around central-bank mandates and keep useful backup material available for client discussion, while avoiding pressure to over-simplify the policy analysis too early.
hidden_assumptions: When people refer to 'the case studies we discussed,' they mean the wider set of examples the team has been informally developing across calls and draft notes, even if only some are currently foregrounded in the outline.
A 'support pack' should include both directly cited evidence and extra backup material, caveats, and optional exhibits that may help in partner or client conversations later.
If analysis is described as 'final,' that means the substantive argument is settled; source formatting, wording refinements, and qualification language can still be completed after handoff.

When someone asks him to 'update the deck,' it is acceptable to continue refining his local working deck first and send it over once his additions are complete, rather than editing directly in the shared master.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'the case studies we discussed' refers to
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to 'the case studies we discussed' or 'the examples we talked through' as if that phrase points to one shared set.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 takes this to mean the example set already built into the approved chapter outline and expected to appear in the main narrative as concise case boxes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 takes this to mean the broader pool of central-bank examples developed across recent team discussions, including additional cases and coordination examples that may appear in backup or be folded into the narrative later.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The two sets overlap on the most salient examples, and both speakers use the phrase collectively without listing items, so the apparent common reference feels routine and does not invite clarification.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that M2 will send the 'final support pack' for the chapter.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects a tightly bounded package limited to citations, short evidence notes, and materials directly used in the current chapter draft.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects a broader bundle that also includes backup slides, extra caveats, alternative evidence, and optional materials that may be useful in review or client discussion even if they are not in the chapter body.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In business coordination settings, 'support pack' sounds like an ordinary shared artifact whose boundaries are assumed to be obvious from context, so neither participant feels a need to define what is inside it.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They use 'final' and 'finalized' to describe sections and handoff materials.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats 'final' as review-ready: integrated into the chapter, fully sourced, and polished enough that internal reviewers can react to substance rather than missing pieces.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 treats 'final' as substantively settled: the analytical position is fixed, but references, wording cleanup, and some caveat language can still be finished afterward.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Experienced project teams often use 'final' loosely during fast-moving handoffs, and each participant assumes the other shares their production norm because both are speaking cooperatively about getting to closure.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that M2 will 'update the deck' before handoff.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects M2 to make changes directly in the shared master deck on the drive so all downstream users see one current file.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 plans to keep refining his own working deck first, then pass it along once his additions and appendix material are in better shape.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both participants assume the working-file convention is already established and too operational to require discussion, so 'update the deck' sounds like straightforward agreement even though they imagine different execution paths.
